context: Only now does he ask who they are. The embraces of Canto 6 were for a fellow Mantuan, not for Virgil.

quote: were ever guided to this mountain
note: Virgil died in 19 BC. No soul came to Purgatory until Christ's death opened the way to Heaven, some fifty years later.

context: Octavian was his name before he took the title Augustus. Virgil died at Brindisi, and the emperor had his body carried to Naples for burial.
He gives his name and his sentence in one breath: shut out of Heaven for lack of faith, not for anything he did.

note: Dante leaves the place unsaid. Commentators take it as the knees or the feet. A moment ago Sordello embraced Virgil as an equal.
Latins means Italians, ancient and modern alike.
Sordello wrote in Provençal, Virgil in Latin, Dante in Italian. Sordello speaks of them as one language, with Latin as its highest form.
God.
After death. Virgil was already in Limbo when he saw Christ come down to free the faithful of the Old Testament (Inferno 4).
Children who died before baptism. The "human sinfulness" is original sin, the guilt inherited from Adam, which baptism washes away.

Faith, hope and charity, which come only by God's grace. "All the others" are the four virtues the ancient philosophers taught: prudence, justice, courage and temperance. The good pagans had these in full.

context: After six cantos on the mountain, the poets are still outside Purgatory itself. Its gate is reached in Canto 9.

note: The souls who wait below the gate may wander the lower slopes as they like.

The law of the mountain. The sun stands for God's grace, and without it the will can do nothing: a soul may stand still or slip back, but not go up. It echoes Christ's words in John's Gospel: walk while you have the light.
Virgil knew every turn of Hell. On this mountain he is a stranger, and has to learn its rules from the souls who live here.

quote: where the border fades more than halfway
note: A line no one reads with confidence. The likeliest sense is that the rim of the hollow is lowest here, so the poets can look in.

A much-debated line. Some read a single bright wood from India; others read indigo, a blue dye, and then a polished wood. Either way it is a list of the richest colors a painter or jeweler had, all outdone by the valley's flowers.
"Hail, Queen": a Latin hymn to the Virgin Mary, sung at evening. The singers call themselves exiled children of Eve, sighing in a valley of tears, which suits these souls exactly.
Sordello this time, not Virgil. He will name the rulers from above, without going down among them.

The emperor ranks above the kings. The whole roll call echoes Sordello's own best-known poem, a lament for a dead lord that scolds the rulers of Europe one by one for cowardice. Here he reviews their sons and successors.

context: He alone does not sing. His neglect of Italy was the charge of Canto 6, and he seems to know it.

note: Usually read as Henry VII, the emperor who came to Italy in 1310 and died in 1313 with his work undone. Rudolf could have healed Italy in time and did not.

quote: the land where the waters rise
note: Bohemia. The Moldau runs through Prague and joins the Elbe, which flows across Germany to the North Sea.
Ottokar II, king of Bohemia from 1253. He was Rudolf's great enemy and died fighting him in battle in 1278. Now he comforts him: old hatreds are over here.
Wenceslaus II, king of Bohemia from 1278 to 1305, still alive at the time of the journey. Dante attacks him again in Paradiso 19.

Philip III of France, called the Bold, king from 1270. He invaded Aragon in 1285, lost his fleet, and died at Perpignan on the retreat. The lily is the fleur-de-lis of the French royal arms, which his defeat dishonored.
Henry I of Navarre, called the Fat, who died in 1274. His daughter Joan married Philip III's son.

context: Son of the one and son-in-law of the other. The two kings grieve less for their own faults than for what he has become.

note: Peter III of Aragon, king from 1276 to 1285, named a few lines on. After the Sicilians rose against the French in 1282, he took the crown of Sicily. Dante gives him unusual praise.

quote: that one with the manly nose
context: Peter of Aragon took Sicily from him, and the two were at war until both died in 1285. Here they sing in harmony.

quote: the young man sitting behind him
note: Usually identified as Alfonso III, Peter's eldest son, who reigned in Aragon for only six years and died young in 1291. Some prefer Peter's youngest son, who never reigned.
Peter's younger sons, both reigning in 1300: James II in Aragon and Frederick in Sicily. They have their father's lands but not his worth, the "better inheritance".

quote: Rarely does human worth rise through the branches
note: The lesson of the whole valley. Virtue does not pass down a family tree. God gives it to each person directly, so that people will ask him for it and not credit their blood.
Charles of Anjou again. His heir was Charles II, called the Lame, who ruled Provence and the kingdom of Naples (Apulia) from 1285 to 1309. Both lands suffer under him.

quote: The plant is as inferior to its seed
note: A riddle in three wives. Charles II falls as far below his father, Charles of Anjou, as Charles of Anjou fell below Peter of Aragon.
Peter of Aragon's widow, daughter of King Manfred (Purgatorio 3). She was still alive in 1300, and has more cause to be proud of her husband than Charles's wives had.
Usually taken as the two wives of Charles of Anjou: Beatrice of Provence and Margaret of Burgundy. This Beatrice has nothing to do with Dante's.
Henry III, king from 1216 to 1272, a pious man and a weak ruler. Sordello's lament had mocked him as a coward. His "better issue" is his son Edward I, a strong king and lawmaker.

William VII of Montferrat, in north-west Italy. He sits lowest because he ranks lowest. In 1290 the rebel city of Alessandria captured him and showed him in an iron cage, where he died in 1292. His son's war of revenge brought ruin on his own lands, Montferrat and the Canavese.
